content.text: Students will learn how to appropriately engage in an academic discussion with classmates.
People have different ideas about what creates a sense of belonging.

In Lesson 12, students will write about what allows people to “see themselves” in a story. In Lesson 17, students will consider what character they’d like to have lunch with. In Lesson 18, students will consider moments from
Look Both Ways
that promote empathy.
Students will prepare to respond during community dialogue in Author’s Chair.
Look Both Ways
, by Jason Reynolds
Unit 1 Lesson 10 Student Edition
Accountable Talk Sentence Stems graphic organizer

Evaluate which vignette in Look Both Ways best demonstrates the importance of belonging by citing text evidence, building on classmates’ interpretations, and analyzing how well discussion evidence supports different claims.
Defend an interpretation about belonging in
Look Both Ways
by using discussion stems, text evidence with location language (page/scene/quote), and clear follow-up questions during a
Fishbowl Conversation
Students will Prepare for a
Fishbowl Conversation
by setting group norms.

Students will evaluate which vignette in Look Both Ways best demonstrates the importance of belonging by citing text evidence, building on classmates’ interpretations, and analyzing how well discussion evidence supports different claims.
Students will defend an interpretation about belonging in
Look Both Ways
by using discussion stems, text evidence with location language (page/scene/quote), and clear follow-up questions during a Fishbowl Conversation.
Students will prepare for a Fishbowl Conversation by setting group norms.
Turn and Talk
Fishbowl Conversations
Quick Write
Turn and Talk
Directions:
The characters in
Look Both Ways

find themselves in many different scenarios and facing many different challenges. Turn and talk with a partner about some of the scenarios we’ve encountered in the book so far. How have they been alike? How have they been different?
Think about the scenarios characters have been in so far. What would Jason Reynolds say about the value of telling these stories?
Conversation Norms
Directions:
Before today’s group discussion, it is important to co-construct the conversation norms the class will follow. Consider the following ideas and questions.
What does strong listening look and sound like?
What counts as evidence for
Look Both Ways
What are respectful ways to disagree or build on someone’s thinking?
Part A: Model Discussion
Directions:
Keep your copy of the
Accountable Talk Sentence Stems
worksheet handy during our discussion. You will use it to record responses and comments during the discussion. This is our discussion prompt:
Which story best shows the reader the importance of belonging? Use evidence from the text to support your answer.
During discussion today, we’re going to follow the
Fishbowl Conversation
protocol. This protocol helps us build meaning together instead of just sharing separate opinions.  Here’s how it works:
The class will be split into two groups. One will sit in a circle in the middle of the room (the inner circle), and the other will sit in a circle around the first group (the outer circle).
Students in the inner circle will have 10 minutes to discuss the question prompts.

While the inner circle group is discussing, the outer circle group will silently take notes on the inner circle’s discussion in order to add to their own thinking and provide responses to points brought up by the inner circle.
After 10 minutes, the groups will switch places, and the new inner circle group will have their turn to discuss the question prompts while the new outer circle group silently takes notes.
Respond to the discussion prompt using these sentence frames:
“The story ‘____’ best shows the reader the importance of belonging.”
“In the text, it says ____. This shows the importance of belonging because ____.”
Reflect on the experience using these sentence frames:
“One idea I heard in the inner circle was ____.”
“As an observer, I noticed ____.”
Reflection
Reflect on your ability to prepare for a group discussion using the
Reflection
routine.
How confident are you in contributing to the
Fishbowl Conversation
Part B: Fishbowl Conversation
Fishbowl Conversation
Outer Circle Task
Directions:

While you are in the outer circle, your job is not just to listen; it is also to evaluate. Identify one speaker’s claim and the reason they gave. Then write whether the evidence they cited actually supports their claim and why or why not.
Speaker’s claim: ___
Evidence they used: ___
Does the evidence support the claim? Why or why not? ___
Check for Understanding
As you discuss and take notes, be sure to:
State a clear central idea that answers the discussion prompt.
Use evidence from the text to support your idea.
Explain relationships between your idea and evidence.
Build on others’ ideas using discussion moves (agree/disagree with reasons, ask a follow-up question, add a new piece of evidence) while keeping comments grounded in the text.
Quick Write
Directions:
Respond to the following question in one to two sentences.
What is one claim you heard during the discussion, and how well was it supported by evidence?

Use this opening to activate students’ prior reading and position them to think about belonging as a theme across multiple scenarios. Students should move beyond recalling events to considering how different experiences shape whether characters feel included, supported, or isolated. This discussion primes students to evaluate which moments most strongly communicate a sense of belonging, a skill they will need during the Fishbowl Conversation.
Turn and Talk
Have students share ideas from their homework for the previous lesson, encouraging them to share the evidence they found to support their ideas.
Say these Directions:
The characters in
Look Both Ways

find themselves in many different scenarios and facing many different challenges. Turn and talk with a partner about some of the scenarios we’ve encountered in the book so far. How have they been alike? How have they been different?
Give students time to discuss with a partner before a brief large-group discussion.
Ask:
Think about the scenarios characters have been in so far. What would Jason Reynolds say about the value of telling these stories?

Jasmine deals with chronic illness. In “Water Booger Bears,” she couldn’t catch up on work: “While she was laid up because she could barely move. It hurt to hold a pen. Hurt to turn a page.” Jason Reynolds would say that this story could help kids with a similar illness feel less alone.
Connection to Today’s Learning
Say:
Jason Reynolds writes about the power and value of storytelling to help people feel a sense of belonging. Today, we’ll look at how different stories in
Look Both Ways
create a sense of belonging.
Teacher Tip

Connect the homework to the idea that teens' experiences change over time. Ask students: “ Do you think the challenges teens face today are similar to or different from the challenges characters face in
Look Both Ways
? Why?”
Students will share moments from their homework that show characters facing challenges.
Conversation Norms
Say these Directions:
Before today’s group discussion, it is important to co-construct the conversation norms the class will follow. Consider the following ideas and questions.
Write each chosen norm on the board for students to see during the discussion.
Say:
Our first norm should be about listening.
Ask
What does strong listening look and sound like?
eyes on speaker, quiet body, taking notes,  waiting for a pause
Say:
Let’s put it in a clear norm: “We listen without interrupting.” That means one voice at a time, and we wait until a speaker finishes before responding.
Say:
Our second norm should be about using evidence. In this unit, we don’t just share opinions; we support them.
Ask:
What counts as evidence for
Look Both Ways
a quote from the book, like a description or dialogue from one of the characters
Say:
Let’s write the norm: “We support our comments with textual evidence.” When you speak, try to include a page number or describe where your evidence is so others can find it.
Say:
Our final norm should be about how we respond. In a strong discussion, we respond to
ideas
, not to
people
Ask:
What are respectful ways to disagree or build on someone’s thinking?
“I agree because ____ ”; “I want to add ____ ”; “I see it differently because ____ ”; “Can you clarify what you meant when you said ____?”
Say:
Let’s write the norm: “We respond to ideas rather than people.” We don’t label someone’s comment as “wrong”; we explain our thinking and use evidence.
Situation
Try this
Struggling with: Understanding conversation norms

Briefly model a “mini turn” using a sentence frame and evidence. Ex. “I think ____ . On page __ , [character’s name] says, “____.” Ex. “I [agree/disagree] with the idea that ____ because the text says ____ .” Ex. “Can you point to a line that supports that?”
Ready for extension: Citing text evidence

Invite students to use the following sentence frames to make two discussion “moves” in one turn ( e.g., build and challenge) while citing evidence during discussion. Ex. “I agree with ____ , and I want to add ____ . On p. __ , [character name or descriptive idea] suggests ____ .” Ex. “Another interpretation is ____ . The quote ‘ ____’ (p. __) makes the reader think ____ .”
Tell students that they can use their own sentence frames if they wish, as long as they convey ideas that address the prompt.
Support students in co-creating Fishbowl Conversation norms that make discussion evidence-based and equitable so everyone can defend interpretations respectfully.
Encourage planning: students can jot a claim + one quote before speaking to reduce pressure and improve clarity.
Post norms in “student action” language (what to do, not just what to be).
Add an explicit evidence norm: “Cite the text so others can find it.”
Add an explicit response norm: “Respond to the idea, then add evidence or a question.”
Turn norms into stems students will actually use.
Model one “agree + evidence” move and one “disagree + evidence” move.
Model one clarifying question that asks for evidence.
I agree because ___ (p. __ ).
I see it differently because ___.
Can you point to where the text shows that?
I want to add on: ___.
Provide sentence frames for multilingual learners based on their proficiency levels as appropriate, and gradually reduce these supports as students become more independent.
Emerging:
"I think ___ shows belonging because ___." / "In the text, ___ shows this."
Expanding:
"I agree with ___ because ___." / "I want to add ___." / "According to the text, ___."
Bridging:
"Building on ___'s idea, ___." / "I see it differently because ___." / "This shows ___, which suggests ___."
If norms stay too broad (“be respectful”) → Prompt: What words can you say when you disagree?
If students don’t cite evidence → Prompt: Add “ In the text . . . ” + page/scene.
Students can restate norms as actions.
Students can say one evidence-based stem aloud.
Students can say one respectful disagreement stem.

Students at different proficiency levels may need to begin at different points within the task. Based on responses, look for opportunities to support and expand student use of academic language, and provide scaffolding as needed.
Emerging:
Shares one opinion with a frame; names one piece of evidence from the text.
Expanding:
Defends an interpretation using discussion stems; cites evidence with a brief explanation.
Bridging:
Defends an interpretation using a full set of academic stems; cites specific evidence; builds on peers' interpretations.
Connection to Today’s Learning
Say:
Reflecting on each other’s ideas helps you process the information to clarify your own ideas better.
Students will participate in co-constructing the conversation norms they will follow during the discussion in this lesson.
Part A: Model Discussion (RL.6.1, SL.6.1.a) (10 minutes)

Use this section to make the expectations for academic discussion visible and concrete. Students should see a clear model of how to state a claim, select relevant textual evidence, and explain how that evidence supports an interpretation about belonging. Emphasize that strong contributions do more than share opinions—they connect ideas to specific moments in the text and prepare students to respond to others. This preparation ensures students enter the Fishbowl ready with a complete, evidence-based idea and a question to extend discussion.
Provide students with the
Accountable Talk Sentence Stems graphic organizer,
and remind them of the following academic discussion prompt.
Say these Directions:
Keep your copy of the
Accountable Talk Sentence Stems
worksheet handy during our discussion. You will use it to record responses and comments during the discussion. This is our discussion prompt:
Which story best shows the reader the importance of belonging? Use evidence from the text to support your answer.
Before you begin the group discussion, explain the structure of the
Fishbowl Conversation
Say:
During our discussion today, we’re going to follow the
Fishbowl Conversation
protocol. This protocol helps us build meaning together instead of just sharing separate opinions. Here’s how it works:
The class will be split into two groups. One will sit in a circle in the middle of the room (the inner circle), and the other will sit in a circle around the first group (the outer circle).
Students in the inner circle will have 10 minutes to discuss the question prompts.

While the inner circle group is discussing, the outer circle group will silently take notes on the inner circle’s discussion in order to add to their own thinking and provide responses to points brought up by the inner circle.
After 10 minutes, the groups will switch places, and the new inner circle group will have their turn to discuss the question prompts while the new outer circle group silently takes notes.
Provide students with the prompts they will be discussing during the
Fishbowl Conversation.
Then model a response using discussion stems and examples (see the sample responses below).
Say:
Imagine this is my prompt: Which story best shows the reader the importance of belonging? Use evidence from the text to support your answer.
The inner circle might discuss the following:

The story “The Low Cuts Strike Again” best shows readers the importance of belonging. In the text, it says, “And it was this, not the cancer but the strain it put on everyone, that formed the Low Cuts. They all cut their hair down to almost bald—a sign of solidarity—and started stealing.” This shows the importance of belonging because the Low Cuts all share the experience of having a parent with cancer. Spending time together helps them feel solidarity, or a sense of belonging, and not being alone. This community is important to them.

The outer circle might then respond as follows: One idea I heard in the inner circle was that the characters in “ The Low Cuts Strike Again” feel a sense of belonging because they all have a parent with cancer. As an observer, I noticed that this speaker used a quote from the text to support their answer.
Provide students with sentence frames to use in the inner and outer circles:
Respond to the discussion prompt using these sentence frames:
“The story ‘____ ’ best shows the reader the importance of belonging.”
“In the text, it says ____ . This shows the importance of belonging because ____ .”
Reflect on the experience using these sentence frames:
“One idea I heard in the inner circle was ____ .”
“As an observer, I noticed ____ .”

By the end of this preparation, students should have at least one clearly articulated claim, a piece of textual evidence with location language, and an explanation of how that evidence supports their thinking. They should also be ready to ask a follow-up question or build on a peer’s idea. This ensures that all students can actively contribute and sustain the discussion rather than relying on spontaneous or unsupported responses.
Instruct students to prepare for the
Fishbowl Conversation
by reviewing their homework connections and preparing textual evidence from both texts to support their ideas.
Help students rehearse defending an interpretation (which story best shows belonging) using a claim–evidence–reasoning structure before the Fishbowl Conversation begins.
Require students to prep one “ready to say” turn: claim + quote/paraphrase + explanation.
Have students underline the key words in their evidence that they will read aloud.
Prompt students to plan one follow-up question they can ask.
Convert “I like this story” into “This story best shows belonging because . . . ”
Strengthen reasoning with connectors: because, this shows, as a result.
Add a comparison nudge: “Compared to ___, this vignette shows ___.”
The story “___” best shows belonging because ___.
On p. __/when ___, the text says/shows ___.
This shows belonging because ___.
A question I have for the group is ___.
Provide sentence frames for multilingual learners based on their proficiency levels as appropriate, and gradually reduce these supports as students become independent.
Emerging:
“My claim is ___.” / “One quote that shows this is ___.”
Expanding:
“My claim is that ___ shows belonging because ___ (quote/paraphrase). This shows ___.”
Bridging:
“My claim is that ___ best shows belonging because ___ (quote, p. __); this shows ___, which connects to the bigger idea that ___.”
Allow students to choose the vignette they feel most confident citing; confidence supports accuracy and participation.
If students have evidence but no explanation → Prompt: Add “ This shows . . . ”
If students explain without evidence → Prompt: Add one quote or exact detail.
Students prepare one complete claim–evidence–reasoning turn.
Students include location language (page/scene).
Students prepare one question to propel discussion.
Students at different proficiency levels may need to begin at different points within the task. Based on responses, look for opportunities to scaffold up or release supports.
Emerging:
Prepares one ‘ready to say’ turn with a frame; names one quote or paraphrase.
Expanding:
Prepares claim + evidence + explanation in a single rehearsed turn.
Bridging:
Prepares a precise claim with cited evidence and connects it to a thematic idea about belonging.

attrs.label: Additional Student Support: Preparing for Discussion

content.text: Situation
Try this
Struggling with: Preparing text evidence
Provide a concrete, four-part checklist and a sentence frame students can reuse in the Fishbowl Conversation. Ex. Checklist:  claim → evidence from
Look Both Ways
→ How do the ideas connect? Claim: What story best shows a sense of belonging? (Write 6–10 words.)

Evidence: Copy one short piece of description or dialogue that shows that idea. Underline two or three key words. Link: Write one sentence explaining the connection using words or phrases such as because, this shows that, or as a result. Sentence frame: “The story ‘____ ’ shows a sense of belonging because ____ . The text supports this on page __ when it says ____. This matters because ____ .”
Ready for extension: Deepening  connections
Say:

Add one more layer to your connection by offering a contrast to the sense of belonging, explaining how one scenario shows a lack of belonging. When Stevie does not stand up for Pia, this shows a lack of belonging. Stevie doesn’t help Pia develop a sense of community, leaving her feeling alone.
Reflection (SL.6.1.a)
Reflect on your ability to prepare for a group discussion using the
Reflection
routine.
How confident are you in contributing to the
Fishbowl Conversation
Part B: Fishbowl Conversation (SL.6.1.a, SL.6.3) (20 minutes)
Support students in sustaining the Fishbowl Conversation by defending interpretations with evidence, building on peers, and asking clarifying questions.
Encourage quieter students to enter with a short prepared contribution (one quote + one sentence explanation).
Inner circle: each turn must include evidence or a request for evidence.
Outer circle: notes must include one claim heard + evidence used + one follow-up question.
After the switch, require new speakers to reference one earlier idea: “Building on . . . ”
Revoice to connect ideas across speakers: “That connects to ___’s point because . . . ”
Press for evidence: “Which line supports that?” “How does that evidence support the claim?” “Is there a stronger example in the text?”
Clarify belonging language: community, solidarity, being seen, being excluded.
Building on ___, I think ___.
The text supports this when ___ (p . __ ).
Can you clarify what you mean by ___?
Do you agree, or does a different moment show something else?
Provide sentence frames for multilingual learners based on their proficiency levels as appropriate, and gradually reduce these supports as students become independent.
Emerging:
“In ___, ___ shows ___.” / “I agree with ___ because ___.”
Expanding:
“Building on ___’s idea, the moment ___ shows that ___ because ___.”
Bridging:
“Building on ___’s claim, the quote ‘___’ shows that belonging is shaped by ___; this raises the question ___?”
If discussion becomes opinion-only → Prompt: Add one text detail.
If students interrupt or jump in → Prompt: Use a stem to enter: “ I want to add . . . ”
Students cite the text at least once while speaking.
Students build on a peer’s idea (not isolated comments).
Students ask at least one clarifying/probing question.

Use this moment to reinforce that citing evidence is necessary but requires deeper thinking. Students must also evaluate how well that evidence supports a claim. Encourage them to listen critically by asking: Does this detail clearly show belonging? Is there a stronger example? This focus helps students move from simply participating in discussion to analyzing the strength of ideas and reasoning.
Students at different proficiency levels may need to begin at different points within the task. Based on responses, look for opportunities to scaffold up or release supports.
Emerging:
Contributes one turn with a frame; cites one detail from the text.
Expanding:
Builds on a peer’s idea; cites a specific moment with explanation.
Bridging:
Sustains discussion with claims, evidence, and clarifying questions; refines or challenges peers’ ideas with text-based reasoning.
Fishbowl Conversations

Engage students in the Fishbowl Conversation protocol. Divide students into the inner circle and outer circle groups. Have the groups switch places after 10 minutes so that all students have the chance to both contribute to and observe a discussion.
Outer Circle Task (SL.6.3)
Say these Directions:

While you are in the outer circle, your job is not just to listen; it is also to evaluate. Identify one speaker’s claim and the reason they gave. Then write whether the evidence they cited actually supports their claim and why.
Display the following note-catcher prompts:
Speaker’s claim: ___
Evidence they used: ___
Does the evidence support the claim? Why or why not? ___
As students engage in the
Fishbowl

, they should practice both contributing and evaluating ideas. Inner circle students should support their claims with relevant, clearly explained evidence, while outer circle students should assess whether the evidence truly supports the claim and be prepared to respond. This dual focus builds students’ ability to both construct and critique arguments, directly supporting collaborative discussion and analytical listening.
Situation
Try this
Struggling with: Inner circle discussion

Give a two-step routine that keeps students focused on stating a claim and offering evidence from the text. Step 1: State a claim. Ex. “The story I think best conveys a sense of belonging is ____ .” Step 2: Prove the claim with details from the text. Ex. “I believe the main reason is ____ . On page __ , the text says ____ .”
Struggling with: Outer circle  note-taking

Give a two-step routine that helps students capture what was said and what evidence supports it. Step 1: Track the conversation. Ex. “They argued that ____ .” Step 2: Prepare one response to share when circles switch. Ex. “I heard someone say ____ , and I can add ____ from
Look Both Ways
Ready for extension: Making connections
Ask:

What are other ways Jason Reynolds creates a sense of belonging in the book? The structure of the book helps create a sense of belonging. Each chapter focuses on a different street and character, creating a sense of continuity.
Check for Understanding
As you discuss and take notes, be sure to:
State a clear central idea that answers the discussion prompt.
Use evidence from the text to support your idea.
Explain relationships between your idea and evidence.
Build on others’ ideas using discussion moves (agree/disagree with reasons, ask a follow-up question, add a new piece of evidence) while keeping comments grounded in the text.
Part A: Model Discussion (RL.6.1, SL.6.1.a)
Students will prepare for the academic discussion.
Part B: Fishbowl Conversation (SL.6.1.a, SL.6.3)
Students will participate in the Fishbowl Conversation.

Use this reflection to reinforce that strong discussions can shift or deepen thinking. Students should identify a specific idea or piece of evidence from a peer that influenced their understanding of belonging and explain why. This helps students recognize the value of listening, evaluating ideas, and revising their thinking in light of new perspectives.
Quick Write
Say these Directions:
Respond to the following question in one to two sentences.
Ask:
What is one claim you heard during the discussion, and how well was it supported by evidence?
Optional Sentence Starter:
“Someone from the other group said ____ . This made me think about ____ .”

Someone from the other group claimed that the Low Cuts did not fully create a sense of belonging because some classmates still felt excluded by them. The speaker supported this idea with details about how other students reacted to the group, which made the claim more convincing.
Students will reflect on an idea shared by a member of another group that changed their thinking.
Have students read “Call of Duty” and take notes in their Journal on the following prompt:
List and describe three things that Ty and Bryson value about their friendship.

"Call of Duty" includes content that some classroom communities may prefer to substitute. If you'd rather not assign this chapter for homework, students can complete the following prompt instead. It preserves the focus on character values and friendship that prepares students for tomorrow's lesson on identity and relationships.
In your
Journal
, respond to the following prompt:

Think about a close friendship in your life or a friendship between two characters from a book, show, or movie you know well. List and describe three things the friends value about their friendship. For each one, briefly explain how you know it matters to them — what they do, say, or share that shows it.

data.subject: ELA

standards.description: Cite textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.

Come to discussions prepared, having read or studied required material; explicitly draw on that preparation by referring to evidence on the topic, text, or issue to probe and reflect on ideas under discussion.
Pose and respond to specific questions with elaboration and detail by making comments that contribute to the topic, text, or issue under discussion.
Delineate a speaker’s argument and specific claims, distinguishing claims that are supported by reasons and evidence from claims that are not.
Adapt speech to a variety of contexts and tasks, demonstrating command of formal English when indicated or appropriate.

Contribute to class, group, and partner discussions by following turn‐taking rules, asking relevant questions, affirming others, adding relevant information and evidence, paraphrasing key ideas, building on responses, and providing useful feedback.
Engage in conversational exchanges and express ideas on familiar topics by asking and answering yes‐no and wh‐ questions and responding using simple phrases.
Contribute to class, group, and partner discussions by following turn‐taking rules, asking relevant questions, affirming others, adding relevant information, and paraphrasing key ideas.

Negotiate with or persuade others in conversations using appropriate register (e.g., to reflect on multiple perspectives) using a variety of learned phrases, indirect reported speech (e.g., I heard you say X, and Gabriel just pointed out Y), as well as open responses.

Negotiate with or persuade others in conversations (e.g., to gain and hold the floor or ask for clarification) using basic learned phrases (e.g., I think..., Would you please repeat that?), as well as open responses.
Negotiate with or persuade others in conversations (e.g., to provide counterarguments) using an expanded set of learned phrases (I agree with X, but...), as well as open responses.
Demonstrate active listening in oral presentation activities by asking and answering detailed questions, with minimal prompting and support.
Demonstrate active listening in oral presentation activities by asking and answering basic questions, with prompting and substantial support.
Demonstrate active listening in oral presentation activities by asking and answering detailed questions, with occasional prompting and moderate support.

data.title: Lesson 10: Look Both Ways, Discussion, Part 1

content.text: How do ordinary moments reveal who we are and how we belong?
